#### 1. diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic, X-linked  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.446)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-418555)

**Proposed mechanism:** PTH1R (HGNC:9060) —LEADS_TO→ Eiken syndrome (MONDO:0010803); PTH1R (HGNC:9060) —DECREASES→ vasopressin signaling pathway (GO:0007221); AVPR2 (HGNC:916) —LEADS_TO→ nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, X-linked (MONDO:0010581); AVPR2 (HGNC:916) —DISRUPTS→ vasopressin signaling pathway (GO:0007221); vasopressin signaling pathway (GO:0007221) —LEADS_TO→ impaired water reabsorption (HP:0011080); impaired water reabsorption (HP:0011080) —LEADS_TO→ polyuria (HP:0000107); impaired water reabsorption (HP:0011080) —LEADS_TO→ polydipsia (HP:0000108). Mutations in PTH1R in Eiken syndrome can indirectly affect water homeostasis, potentially by modulating pathways related to vasopressin signaling. In contrast, X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is directly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AVPR2 gene, which encodes the vasopressin V2 receptor, leading to impaired water reabsorption and polyuria/polydipsia. The convergence occurs at the level of the vasopressin signaling pathway and its downstream effects on water balance.

**How to falsify it:** If genetic studies reveal that mutations in PTH1R do not impact the vasopressin signaling pathway or water homeostasis in a manner consistent with Eiken syndrome, or if AVPR2 mutations are found to have a gain-of-function effect leading to X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: gnomAD analysis showing common variants (AF > 0.01) in either PTH1R or AVPR2 associated with these phenotypes would question their role as rare disease genes.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role in water homeostasis, even if mediated through different primary genes (PTH1R vs AVPR2), could lead to novel therapeutic strategies targeting common downstream pathways for managing fluid balance disorders. Identifying indirect effects of PTH1R on vasopressin signaling could reveal new therapeutic targets for Eiken syndrome that also impact water regulation.
